On 16 October 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, the dentist William Morton put a patient to sleep with ether vapour while the surgeon John Collins Warren removed a lump from his neck. The patient felt no pain. The show convinced the medical world that surgery without pain was possible.

Before this, surgeons had to work on conscious, screaming patients, so speed was everything and most deep operations were impossible. A Georgia doctor, Crawford Long, had used ether in 1842 but did not publish until later.

News crossed the Atlantic within weeks, and ether was being used in London by December 1846. In 1847 the Scottish doctor James Young Simpson introduced chloroform. Queen Victoria later took chloroform in childbirth, which made pain relief respectable.

Anaesthesia let surgeons work slowly and carefully. Combined with Joseph Lister's antiseptic methods from 1867, it made modern surgery possible. Morton spent the rest of his life fighting others for credit.
